content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to alleviate the temporal inconsistency within a sequence of frames that are processed individually. Compared to previous approaches, the proposed framework claimed data efficiency by avoiding the usage of raw image for motion estimation and better motion representation through tri-frame input as their main contributions. On the popular benchmarks, the proposed framework achieves marginally better quantitative result and favorable results on the user-study.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weakness:
- Inconsistent claims and formulation. (1) The paper claims not to use raw images for motion representation, while Eqn 3-5 clearly takes the raw images as input. (2) Page 5, the paper claims to use (P_{t-1}, P_t, P_{t+1}) for motion estimation, while the framework figure 2 uses (O_{t-1}, P_{t}, P_{t+1}) and Eqn 3 uses (O_t and O_{t-1}). Thus, I don't know what the author actually implemented in practice.

- Lack of novelty. The proposed loss has four terms (Eqn 8) and only the first term L_{fg} is incrementally new and the fourth term L_{constancy} is a minor extension, compared to Lai et al.

- Incremental performance. The quantitative result is marginally better than others, while noting that the metric is a rough proxy for the task, It's hard for me to tell the difference from Lai et al. for the qualitative results in Fig. 7.

- Confusing ablation study on the proposed terms. The supplementary shows the warping error for different combinations of terms on the scale of 0.1 (Fig. 8) while Table 1 shows the error on the scale of 0.001. In addition, it'll be good to have ablation study for Eqn 7 to see the importance of long-term comparison.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As explained in the weakness above, my major concern about the paper is that its claims and formulations are inconsistent. The claimed contribution/framework figure and method formulation are talking about different things. Thus, I have no idea what the proposed method really is. Even if the method formulation can be corrected, the proposed framework's novelty is incremental compared to Lai et al.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has an interesting idea for directly working on processed frames without using raw images. However, the formulation still uses the raw images, which is inconsistent with the claim. Even if the formulation can be easily corrected, the novelty is limited as only one term can be viewed as marginally novel. In addition, the quantitative and qualitative results do not seem to be significantly better than the prior art. In terms of the writing, I'd suggest authors to reuse the notations and terms from Lai et al., making it easier for readers to understand its novelty.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed an algorithm to learn a temporal consistency correction to solve the inconsistency issues in processed videos. To solve this problem, this paper conducts motion estimation from three adjacent frames instead of two to get a more robust estimation. To regularize the temporal consistency, this paper employs local neighborhood losses and temporal consistency losses. Quantitative results show that the outputs of this work are preferred by more users, and have less temporal warping error than the previous blind video consistency methods on DAVIS and VIDEVO datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The proposed method directly operates on the processed videos.
+ The method is task agnostic.
+ Achieve good competitive performance in terms of quantitative and qualitative experiments.
+ This paper conducts detailed ablation studies about the influence of loss functions and choice of different optical flow estimation networks, which could help other researchers in future design.

Weakness:
- The major difference between this paper and the previous ones are not too much: extending two frames to three might bring up the temporal consistency, while the influence of frame number is not fully verified in the paper.
- The difference of the outputs of this paper and the previous methods are not too obvious. Just evaluating from the qualitative results shown in the paper, both Lai and DVP's results look good to me. The video provided in the supplementary materials are too short with quick switch, so in the limited playtime, my eyes can only tell that Lai's, DVP's and "Ours" are at the same level of consistency. Besides, this proposed method is a little bit slower than "Lai et al" in terms of runtime.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Paper quality:
This paper is well-written with clear introduction of the background knowledge and the methodologies. It also provides some necessary ablation studies in the supplementary material to help justify the experimental setups of this paper.

Clarity: 
This paper is presented clearly with proper figures and annotations. 

Originality: 
This paper is somewhat novel. 

Reproducibility: 
The author mentioned that the code and trained models will be released upon acceptance. Once released, it will be much easier to reproduce the results in this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I would consider this paper slightly below the acceptance threshold due to the weakness in novelty. I would like to hear from the other reviewer's comments as well as the author's feedback to adjust my final rating.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper a blind video temporal inconsistency correction method is introduced. Unlike most existing post-processing type of works that require raw/processed video pair, the proposed method consumes processed video only at test time, making it more useful in practice, while at the same time, this poses a challenge to the motion estimation due to the presence of inconsistent noise in the optical flow for processed frames. 

To alleviate the problem, the authors design a two branch neural network architecture to process motion and content separately. A key contribution is to learn consistent optical flow from three consecutive frames instead of two, as such strategy overcomes the equal contribution of frames in motion estimation, and allows the network to develop a sense of rigidity to distinguish consistent content from a set of temporally inconsistent frames. Both raw and processed frames are used to supervise / guide the correction of temporal inconsistency, as the authors devised a set of losses to facilitate the model training, including the flow gradient, image reconstruction, perceptual similarity, as well as the temporal consistency losses. 

Qualitative / quantitative evaluation, user study, and runtime comparison on various video temporal inconsistency correction tasks demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach. Some ablation study was also conducted to justify the decision on loss functions and flow network selection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Novel modeling of optical flow on temporally inconsistent videos as the sum of consistent optical flow and inconsistent noise, paving the road for tri-frame motion estimation that is robust to inconsistency in video frames. 
- The introduction of flow gradient loss (spatial-temporal) defined on the raw and predicted / corrected frames, outperforming the raw optical flow based loss function. 
- Results on various video temporal inconsistency correction tasks are presented. Good balance between model performance and efficiency. On par with SOTA task agnostic approaches while requiring processed video only at test time. 

Weaknesses:
- The manuscript may benefit from more clarity on the description on input settings, details on ConvLSTM, details on the optical flow network in motion estimation module and loss functions, and training procedure. Please see feedback for the next question for elaboration. 
- The work is largely built upon Lai et al., sharing many important details such as the model building blocks, loss functions, among others. While the new contributions are summarized above under "Strength", overall the work is moderately incremental from the technical perspective.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the work may benefit from improved clarity on the following few aspects:
- Firstly, there are a few potential notation inconsistencies / typos in the manuscript
	- In Fig 2: inputs are denoted as P_{t+1}, P_t, and O_{t-1}, whereas based on the main text, this should be three consecutive frames from the input/unprocessed video only (thus last frame should be P_{t-1} instead). 
	- If so it would be helpful if the authors could clarify how the ConvLSTM block work as part of the content branch, specifically, what are fed into the block to make it recurrent. Neither in the main text or the model architecture drawing in Fig. 2 is such info made clear.
- The claim on not relying on unprocessed videos is misleading and should always be accompanied with "at test time". From the first glimpse the readers may walk away with the impression that raw videos are not required at all, whereas in reality the model does need both raw and processed video counterparts for training / fine-tuning. 
- Optical flow network: for the content block, PWCNet was selected and fine-tuned as part of the training process. The specifics of the "of" network in the loss functions, on the other hand, are less clear. Is it a fix-weight FlowNet 2.0 (Ilg et al 2017)? Is the motion branch used in the loss calculation, and if not, how does the motion estimation network learn to predict inconsistency-robust flow information without direct supervision on the flow prediction? 
- It is unclear what "Trained" means in Table 1. Please consider clarifying this. 

Quality: 
- The ablation study could be done more thoroughly: for example, how important is the perceptual loss L_p? 
- The work needs more justification on the network design, such as the importance of the ConvLSTM. 

Novelty: see comments for the previous questions (weaknesses). 

Reproducibility: 
- See ConvLSTM comment above.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a task agnostic temporal consistency correction framework that delivers on-par performance with SOTA works yet relying on processed video only at test time. Nevertheless, on the technical side the work is mostly built upon Lai et al. and there are a couple of clarity issues that need to be addressed before the work can be accepted.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a novel method for correcting videos to be temporally consistent.  The method is applied to videos produced using image translation tasks applied frame-by-frame to video.  Such methods may result in flickering as the image translation is not guaranteed to be temporally consistent.  The proposed method is blind to the image translation task and does not require the original unprocessed video.  The paper proposes a tri-frame approach which estimates two optical flow fields, from which the consistent motion is identified.  A ConvLSTM is also used to preserve consistency through longer videos.  Experimental results demonstrate the method is effective to produce more temporally consistent results across a range of image translation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Temporal coherence of processed video is an important, and challenging problem.  As effectively argued in the paper, it is becoming increasingly popular to apply image translation filters to video, but these are applied on a frame-by-frame basis, resulting in flickering artifacts due to temporal inconsistency of the translation.  Similar challenges arise in enhancement of video for example in a camera’s image signal processor.  

The paper has the following strengths: 

1.	Formulation of the problem of video temporal consistency in a task-independent way that does not require unprocessed video.  Whilst previous literature has sought solutions to this problem using the unprocessed video, this paper does not require the unprocessed video which makes the method applicable to a wide set of use cases.  This feature of the paper also has good novelty.

2.	The strategy taken is interesting, using a triframe approach to extract two temporally successive optical flow fields, from which the consistent flow can be identified.  The dual branch architecture is a logical approach to identify consistent optical flow and use this in a reconstruction branch focussing on content.  While it appears the losses have appeared in the literature, their combination is shown to be effective (including results in the supplementary material). 

3.	Experimental results are shown to be effective, measured quantitatively as well as qualitatively through user studies.  The majority of users preferred the results produced by the proposed method; although results by Lai et al. were a close second in some experiments.
The incorporation of the video content into the paper itself was helpful to see the effect of the processing.

Weaknesses include:

1.	Clarity.  The paper has a number of areas that could be improved for clarity.  As the question below asks about clarity, details are provided there.  

2.	Optical flow networks used.  It’s clear that accurate optical flow is important for the method to produce good results.  However, the paper uses some rather old optical flow networks (e.g. PWCNet from 2018).  It would be interesting to know why more modern optical flow methods like RAFT weren’t used – would such networks improve results?  Please note, this reviewer is not asking for additional experiments. 

3.	Missing quantitative comparisons to DVP (Lei et al.).  These seem to be missing from Table 1.  The supplementary material gives some justification in terms of computational complexity, but curiously, also argues that the temporal warping error isn’t a useful way to compare the proposed method to DVP.  It raises the question if the temporal warping error is a useful way to compare the proposed method to Lai et al. and Bonneel et al. in Table 1.  Is the temporal warping error useful or not?  The reviewer found this confusing and therefore had less confidence in Table 1 as a result.  The user studies may be more effective.  Why was it possible to provide results for DVP in Figure 6 but not Table 1?  The reviewer found this approach inconsistent.  Perhaps this could be addressed in the author response.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Below is a list of issues for correction:

a.	Use of the word “raw”.  This was particularly confusing for this reviewer, as “raw” in computational photography refers to data captured by an image sensor, normally using a color filter array and requires processing by an image signal processor (ISP) to produce a frame.  However, the paper is not mean “raw” in this context, but instead in the context of unprocessed frames.  It would be much clearer to use the phrase “unprocessed” as in “original unprocessed video” throughout the paper.  This video consists of RGB frames and not raw data captured from the imaging sensor.  This is important because these issues of flickering exist in ISPs as well; conceivably the proposed method could be used to correct for this.  

b.	Use of the unprocessed video and notational inconsistency.  The paper makes a strong claim that it does not require the unprocessed video to improve temporal consistency.  But in the paragraph above Figure 2, when describing the proposed approach, the paper states, “This learned motion representation is then processed with the content of unprocessed videos in a branched network…”  This does not appear to be correct, as the unprocessed videos are unavailable in this paper.  Instead what the paper appears to be trying to say is that the learned motion representation is then processed with the content of temporally stabilized videos”?  

c.	Relatedly, on Page 5 the paper says “The proposed model takes in three consecutive frames P_{t-1}, P_t, P{t+1} but Figure 2 actually shows something different, with O_{t-1} being an input, not P{t-1}.   This creates confusion for the reader on the inputs to the method and how it works. 

d.	The claim of not requiring the unprocessed video could be clarified.  It’s true the proposed method doesn’t require this at inference, but the unprocessed video is required to train the network as it is used in some of the terms in the loss. 

e.	Figure 4 is confusing to this reviewer.  The modified optical flow looks very different compared to the original optical flow.  While the Unprocessed and processed optical flow field look consistent in the lower row of the figure, they bear such little resemblance to the original flow fields it raises concerns of the accuracy of the modified flow.  This experiment would be more convincing if the ground truth optical flow could also be visualized.

f.	It wasn’t clear how the optical flow is incorporated in the network in Figure 2.  A plus sign is used – are the flow fields added in somehow to the content features?  It would appear concatenation would be a more likely strategy but its unclear as described.

g.	It wasn’t clear what the “factorized” user study did – is that looking at naturalness, quality, consistency, etc?

h.	There are other areas for improvement including typos, these are described below 

Smaller issues: 

•	In the related work, the paper says there are two streams of processing.  The first reformulates the problem with temporal information.  But it seems the second is also relying on temporal information.  Perhaps the first stream could be renamed (e.g. video-to-video translation) to better differentiate from the second stream.  As currently formulated, the two streams seem too similar. 

•	Page 4, please change “ant” to “and”

•	Figure 7 caption, please change “generate” to “generated”

•	Table 1 may be clearer if values are reported with 1x10^-3 so three decimal places are used.  For example, on VIDEVO there are two methods with error 0.0006 which appears as a tie but the paper lists the proposed method as superior.  This may be the case but it’s hard to tell as there aren’t enough values beyond the value of 6.  

•	Unusual word choices

o	“Temporal flicker” seems redundant to this reviewer.  Flicker is already temporal.  Maybe the word “temporal” can be removed? 

o	Page 2, “jagged videos” – in what way is the video “jagged”?  Maybe the word “flickering” could be used here

o	Page 3, “hectic” is an unusual word choice.  Maybe the word “taxing” could be used?

o	Page 4, “tangible” – how is the motion representation tangible?  This word could be removed for clarity.

o	Page 5, “justify” – perhaps “support” would be a better word choice

o	Page 6, “succeeding” – it appears the paper means “preceeding”? 

The novelty of the method is good, the network proposed appears to be original, and the use of two optical flow fields to identify consistent flow is a good idea.

Reproducibility is hindered by the lack of clarity.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper is addressing an important and understudied problem that occurs frequently when applying image translation networks to video content.  The proposed method appears to be an advance in approaching this problem, not requiring the unprocessed videos at runtime.  The reviewer is impressed by the paper and the results are appealing.  However, the paper is let down by many issues around clarity.   Some of these issues may be easy to address in a revision.  A significantly revised version of this paper would make for a nice contribution to the literature.  However, given the larger number of issues overall in the paper in its present form, the reviewer is concerned the paper isn’t ready for ICLR and may benefit from more time for careful revision.  The reviewer will maintain an open mind and looks forward to hearing in the author rebuttal.

content.title: Learning Task Agnostic Temporal Consistency Correction
content.TL;DR: This work provides a general framework for task agnostic video temporal consistency correction capable of producing visually pleasing and temporally consistent videos without the requiring their unprocessed counterparts.
content.abstract: In many video restoration/translation tasks, image processing operations are naively extended to the video domain by processing each frame independently. This disregard for the temporal connection in video processing often leads to severe temporal inconsistencies. State-of-the-art techniques that address these inconsistencies rely on the availability of unprocessed videos to siphon consistent video dynamics to restore the temporal consistency of frame-wise processed videos. We propose a novel general framework for this task that learns to infer consistent motion dynamics from inconsistent videos to mitigate the temporal flicker while preserving the perceptual quality for both the temporally neighboring and relatively distant frames. The proposed framework produces state-of-the-art results on two benchmark datasets, DAVIS and videvo.net, processed by numerous image processing applications in a frame-wise processing manner. The code and the trained models will be released upon acceptance.
